items.question: How do you assess robot hardware compared with human bodies?
items.object: Robot hardware compared with human bodies
items.answer: I think robot hardware is really inferior compared to human bodies. And there's no humanmade technology that compares to this path.
quotes: Robot hardware is really inferior compared to human bodies. And there's no humanmade technology that compares to this path.

items.question: How close do you think we are to building an AI smarter than you?
items.object: The timeline for AI smarter than Jürgen Schmidhuber and the limitations of physical AI
items.answer: From a cosmic perspective, we are as close as we were in the 1970s when I first wished. So we are very close. But is it going to be a couple of years or a couple of decades? I'm not totally sure about that because true AI is not just the AI behind the screen, which is working very well and which is passing the Turing test. True AI is also real robots, real machinery outside of the screen, in the real world, in the physical world, and that's not working as well. The hardware in the real world has lots of limitations that human bodies don't have, and we still have a way to go to be able to compete with human bodies in physical AI.

items.question: Why did the ChatGPT moment and recent AI results seem less surprising to you than to people outside neural network research?
items.object: The ChatGPT moment and the predictability of recent AI progress
items.answer: Not really. Not to the extent that it surprised people who had no contact to neural networks and artificial neural networks in the previous decades. Suddenly there was a ChatGPT moment and suddenly people started being interested in that thing, which they had never seen before. They didn't know that there was a long history of large language models and an even longer history of basic insights and algorithms for training these large language models that goes back to the previous millennium. For a guy who was in the center of all of that, it was much easier to predict that than for someone who had totally different interests.

items.question: How do you assess the Gödel machine as an approach to recursive self-improvement?
items.object: The Gödel machine as an approach to recursive self-improvement
items.answer:
In 2003, we had a mathematically optimal way of generating self-improvements by a machine that has some software and is interacting with an environment. This environment sometimes punishes you or provides reward, and you want to maximize the sum of all the rewards in your life until the end of your life and minimize the sum of the pain signals. There's an initial software in that machine, and this machine can in principle write programs that modify the initial software.

But before it modifies itself like that, it first has to prove—which means there's a proof search in the software—that the modification caused by the execution of this particular program is useful in the sense that it will lead to more expected reward than the alternative, which would be not to execute this program. Then it has to generate a formal proof, which was called the Gödel machine.

It is less practical than certain other things that we did, like neural networks that change their own weight matrix by running a learning algorithm on the network itself. That is what we started in 1992, and that's currently more or less the most popular kind of self-modification and self-reference.

There's an initial software in that machine, and this machine can in principle write programs that modify the initial software.

items.question: How do you assess neural-network meta-learning as the current approach to recursive self-improvement?
items.object: Neural-network meta-learning as an approach to recursive self-improvement
items.answer:
I see most of the current self-improving systems as scaled-back versions, toned-down versions, of the Gödel machine of 2003, the mathematically optimal thing. They are more like what we had earlier: neural networks where you have the weights, and the program of a neural network is basically the weight matrix. Recurrent networks, for example, are general-purpose computers, because on a recurrent neural network you can implement the processing unit of your Apple laptop or something like that.

If you have certain instructions that allow you to modify the weights itself, then you can basically run arbitrary learning algorithms on the network, which has to see the errors or negative reward signals that are coming in. That has to be part of the input, which is essential. That's what we did in the early '90s. Back then compute was so expensive, 10 million times more expensive than today, that we could do only little tiny toy experiments. Today you can really show that methods like that can learn to generalize and learn new tasks much faster than if you don't have this meta-learning capacity. This is currently the most popular way of doing recursive self-improvement.

However, I have to admit that it is limited because the learning algorithm is invented through gradient descent. Everything is differentiable, and then the whole network learns through gradient descent to generate weight changes that are better than what's caused by gradient descent.

items.question: How do you think the emergence of AI and recursive self-improvement will look in hindsight from a cosmic perspective?
items.object: The emergence of AI and recursive self-improvement on a cosmic timescale
items.answer: From a cosmic perspective, it will look just like a blip. There was no self-improvement and no real AI, and then there was AI. From a cosmic perspective, this is also true for all of civilization. Civilization started roughly 13,000 years ago, and before that there was no artificial intelligence. Only 13,000 years later, there was artificial intelligence. Basically, the first guy who had agriculture 13,000 years ago and domestication of the animals was almost the same guy who had the first AI. The 13,000 years of civilization are just one-millionth of world history, which is about 13.8 billion years. It's just a flash in world history. In hindsight, it will look like civilization occurred almost at the same time as AI occurred because over these past 13,000 years, more and more stuff was automated, more and more of agriculture was automated, and more and more human labor was automated. At some point, thinking started to become automated a couple of hundred years ago. First the calculators, then the calculators became less expensive, then they became faster, and now you can calculate much more than 100 years ago for the same price. Then suddenly it was there. From this global perspective, it's really like there was nothing and suddenly there was a lot.

items.question: Why do you consider efficiency fundamental to intelligence in self-improving AI systems?
items.object: Intelligence and efficiency in self-improving AI systems
items.answer: Whenever we are talking about intelligence, we basically are talking about laziness. An intelligent being wants to be lazy. It wants to achieve whatever it does with the least possible effort, with the least possible energy consumption. All of our self-improving systems have this extra reward for being efficient. In other words, they have an extra cost every time they wake up a neuron and use energy to wake up that neuron or use energy to do other things. All the computational costs and the other energy costs have to be taken into account in the objective function that our self-improving systems are optimizing.

items.question: How do you think AI labs should approach using pretrained language models to improve their own code?
items.object: Using pretrained language models to improve their own code
items.answer: Today you use large pre-trained systems, large language models that have already read a lot of papers about coding, of course. A modern way of using a pre-trained model like that is you let it code something, and you only improve the way it codes or recodes its own code. That's now a pretty obvious way of doing it, and quite a few labs are interested in exactly that. Of course, you have to have safeguards so it doesn't rewrite its own code in a way that is totally stupid and makes things worse rather than better. There are ways of dealing with that.

items.question: How do you assess the generality of an AI research approach that relies on models pre-trained on human-generated data?
items.object: Reliance on models pre-trained on human-generated data
items.answer:
I think it's a reasonable approach. It's not the most general approach in the sense that if you rely on anything that is pre-trained on human-generated data, then you are ignoring many of the other possibilities.

Look at our current large language models: they are super biased towards humans. Why? Because they are trained on all the data on the worldwide web. All the data on the worldwide web is there for the only reason that at least one person at some point thought this is interesting from a human perspective. All this material that at least someone thought is interesting is used to train the systems, and they are for that reason super biased towards human language, towards videos that humans find interesting, towards behavior that humans find interesting, and so on. They are very aligned in a certain way with humans. Maybe they are more aligned with certain humans than with others. Nevertheless, there's a tremendous human bias.

items.question: Why do you see artificial curiosity, through which agents collect their own training data, as the future of AI?
items.object: Artificial curiosity and agents that generate their own world-model training data
items.answer:
Have an artificial scientist who is living in some unknown environment and tries to build a model of the world by just predicting the consequences of its actions, and then uses the model of the world for planning. Such an agent will have to create through its own actions the data that trains the world model. Suddenly you have something like an artificial scientist who, through its own actions, generates the data on which the world model is being trained. This is much more like what humans do, what babies do. Babies don't learn by downloading the web or something. They learn by predicting the consequences of their actions. If they move their fingers like that, then the video changes, which comes in through the cameras, and they learn to predict these changes. That's how they learn about the physics of the world and about how the world works and how their fingers work and everything.

They are being trained on a lot of data that is not on the worldwide web, collected through their own experiments. It's exactly the kind of data that the baby needs to better understand what it can do and what it needs to maximize its own reward. All of the data collected on the worldwide web seems to be a lot, but it's just a tiny, tiny, tiny fraction of all the possible data that you could collect out there through your own experiments.

The future of AI is going to lie in such systems that, through their own actions, through artificial curiosity as I called it in 1990, collect all the data that is used to train the world models. These world models will not depend on human language, and they will be very focused in many ways on this particular robot that is collecting the data. Of course, it is going to communicate with other robots living in different environments and incorporate that knowledge so it can better generalize, and so on. Suddenly you have a situation where the systems are going to be much less human-biased.

items.question: How do you explain what drives scientific curiosity through your formal theory of fun and creativity?
items.object: The formal theory of fun and creativity as an explanation of scientific curiosity
items.answer:
Twenty years ago I wrote this paper about the formal theory of fun and creativity, which is about exactly that. What should an artificial scientist or any scientist or any artist or any comedian do when its main needs, like eating three times a day, are satisfied and it has extra time to do stuff? What do you do? You listen to music or maybe compose your own music, generate art, or you are a scientist who not only is trying to solve problems given to you by other people. You also try to invent your own new problems. Ask your own questions. Not just answer questions given to you by somebody else, but invent your own new good questions. That's what scientists do.

All of science is about two things. It's not only taking an existing question and investing a lot of time into solving it and finding an answer. It's also inventing the good questions. The basic principle is very simple. An artificial scientist, or any scientist—in my point of view, a human scientist as well—is driven by one simple thing: try to find through your actions your own self-invented experiments, data that has the property that in the data there is some regularity, some pattern that you didn't know but can quickly learn. You didn't know it, but you can quickly learn it because it's at the limit of what you already almost understand, near the horizon of what you don't know and what you know.

You generate this data through your own actions, through your experiments, the sequences of actions which are experiments. The data comes in, and if there is something interesting in the data, what does that mean? It means there's a pattern in there which you didn't know of. All patterns mean there's some way of compressing those things in space and time. You're not talking about time right here, to make things not too complicated. To compress the patterns in a way that you didn't know before: before you understood the regularity and the pattern coming in, you needed so many internal bits and hidden units and so on to encode it. Afterwards, after you learn to see the pattern, after you learn to compress it, you need so many fewer. The difference between before and after, that's the fun that you have. That's just a real number which says how much internal joy this scientist now has from realizing, “Oh, there is a regularity that I didn't know in the data which is coming in. It tells me something about gravity.” Then this becomes the reward of the controller who's generating the actions that lead to the data. The controller is motivated to generate more and more experiments that lead to insights about the world that it didn't have before.

Everything that it understands becomes boring. Then it wants to create more complicated experiments. After it has grabbed the low-hanging fruits, it wants more complicated experiments. Maybe the same baby which first learned about gravity when it was a little being, maybe a year old or something, is 20 years later working at the particle collider at CERN and is part of the team that discovers the Higgs boson. The only difference is that the experiments are more expensive.

items.question: How do you understand the capabilities of the artificial scientists that already exist today?
items.object: Existing artificial scientists and neural networks for chemistry
items.answer:
We don't have the same kind of ChatGPT moment yet for these artificial scientists. But to a certain extent, they already exist, and they are being used in lots of special applications.

For example, in chemistry you have lots of pairs of inputs and outputs, and you train your neural network to predict these new substances given the previous inputs. Over time, if you show it millions of experiments, it learns to become an artificial chemist, an intuitive chemist. It's not a chemist who understands all these reactions from first principles, from valence electrons or whatever. It just becomes an intuitive chemist that better understands what can be done in chemistry.

Then you have certain objectives. For example, you want to create a material that is twice as efficient as the best thing known so far, maybe an insecticide or something. You can say, “Okay, let's have a desired output like that,” which encodes that it should be twice as efficient as the best thing I know. Then you can work the whole chemistry backwards and look at the input side and say, “How much should I change my experiment, which is visible at the input side, to get this thing that I would like to see, to fulfill my wish?” Then the chemist will basically give you a suggestion.

items.question: What do you see as the promise of the KAUST project using metal MOFs to extract carbon dioxide from the air?
items.object: KAUST's project using metal MOFs to extract carbon dioxide from the air
items.answer: At KAUST we have an interesting project where the goal is to use certain patented structures, metal MOFs they're called. The goal is to extract carbon dioxide from thin air, which is important for improving the climate. At the moment all of that is very expensive, and the goal is to make it so cheap that you really can make a dent and maybe improve the global warming situation. That is one of the potential applications, and there are lots of applications in all kinds of chemistry fields.

items.question: Why do you think robot hardware still falls short of the human body for everyday tasks like cleaning a kitchen?
items.object: Robot hardware compared with the human body
items.answer: Back then that didn't work, and it still doesn't work because robot hardware is really inferior compared to human bodies. There's no handmade technology—no humanmade technology—that compares to this hand. This hand is full of sensors, millions of little sensors and little cables that connect to the control center. I wouldn't even know where to put all these cables in an artificial hand. The crazy thing is, you harm it, you cut it, and it starts healing itself. This is super advanced technology. We have nothing like that in man-made tech. That's the reason why the robots in the movies are all played by humans, because humans are much better robots.

items.question: Why do you consider physical mastery of the real world essential to artificial general intelligence?
items.object: Physical mastery of the real world as a requirement for AGI
items.answer: For me, you can't have AGI just behind the screen. You can have a superhuman chess player behind the screen and something that passes the Turing test, but if it doesn't master the real world, it's not an AGI. It's just maybe a fancy text editor behind the screen, or something that has an idea of how this robot should move or whatever, but it's not the real thing. If you want to master the real world through a real AGI, a physical AGI, so much more has to be done. Our robots have to become much better than the limited stuff that we have today.

items.question: How do you assess the economics of today's massive investments in GPUs for data centers?
items.object: The economics of massive GPU data-center investments
items.answer: I think we can easily predict how compute per dollar is going to evolve. It's probably going to stay like what we have seen for decades now: a factor of 10 every five years, roughly like that. That means the guys who are investing a thousand billion dollars into GPUs for data centers today, within the next five years, are going to lose 900 billion dollars. There's no business model that can recuperate that loss, which already is an indication of the coming crash, maybe.

items.question: How do you assess the argument that growing demand for AI compute will justify today's massive investments in data centers?
items.object: The economics of massive investment in AI data centers
items.answer:
I think maybe there will be more and more demand for compute, but somebody has to pay for it, right? If it turns out that those guys who are currently paying are losing a lot of money, at the moment a couple of companies are investing hundreds of billions per year—so in total maybe a trillion per year or something like that—into GPUs for data centers.

These companies used to be nimble software companies. They had a little team improving some operating system and then rolling it out for billions of people who had their own phones and their own computers to run the operating system. Suddenly they're providing clouds and data centers, and they have to become like utilities, like electricity companies, and invest in nuclear power plants and gas turbines and whatever. Suddenly the free cash flow of these companies goes down from 100 billion down to 10 billion or maybe minus 10 billion, like for some of these companies.

At the moment, while everybody is trying to get market share, these services are really not efficient in the sense that the guys providing the services are losing a lot of money. It doesn't show up in the price-earnings ratio because the free cash flow, which really should be considered, is not showing up there. All these companies are getting less and less efficient. At some point they will have to stop. They're taking on debt to finance even more data centers, and this will be possible only to a certain extent. Then these companies will become less and less valuable because they misinvested the money.

At some point, sooner or later, if you can't pay for all these services, if the entire economy is not set up to pay for all these services because compute isn't cheap enough yet, and people want to compensate for it by buying even more computers, if you have a situation like that which doesn't lead to a profitable economy, then it's going to disappear due to the laws of supply and demand.

items.question: Why do you think big companies' current investments in AI computing infrastructure are likely to backfire?
items.object: Big companies' current AI infrastructure investments
items.answer: A stupid way would be just wait a little bit—wait for five years, then compute is going to be 10 times cheaper and you'll be able to do the same thing for one-tenth of the price, or wait 10 years and you'll be able to do the same thing for 1% of the price. But of course the big companies say, “If I wait until the others do it, then I will lose maybe my market share, or I miss out on the opportunity to be the first to have a true AGI.” In that case, once they have a true AGI that can solve everything, they can take over the world, and the investment will be nothing compared to the value of that. But I think all of these outlooks are overoptimistic, and probably we will see that the current way of investing a lot in computers that aren't fast enough yet is going to backfire.

items.question: Why do you think recursive self-improvement will be difficult for large AI companies to turn into a lasting competitive moat?
items.object: Recursive self-improvement as a competitive moat for large AI companies
items.answer: Everybody's cooking with the same water, and almost all of the important algorithms in AI were not invented at big companies or whatever. They were invented at little labs without much funding. Especially the recursive self-improvement stuff and the basic ideas for that all come from little labs, academic labs. Any company that wants to somehow grab that and make it its own doesn't have a moat because there are all these other PhD students out there who are super excited about recursive self-improvement. There's no way to keep a little advantage there for long enough to make a lot of money. I think it will be very difficult for the huge companies to be very profitable in this business.

items.answer: Nobody knows exactly. items.question: Why do you consider the AI alignment efforts of the 2010s misguided?
items.object: AI alignment efforts of the 2010s
items.answer:
I remember in the 2010s we had lots of these safety conferences and alignment conferences, and people writing letters that certain types of recursive self-improvement should be forbidden. Of course, I never signed any of these letters. I think all of these approaches were misguided in many ways. This whole alignment business means that there is somebody who decides what is the nature of this alignment. How do I align these AIs to the needs of humans? But if you have 10 different humans in one room, they all have different needs and different opinions about what is good for humans and what is not good. This whole perspective is dominated by the idea that you give one objective function to this AI which it is supposed to optimize, and that's the alignment that you create through that.

On the other hand, since 1990 or so we have built these artificial scientists which are not really aligned much with anything because all the time they invent their own new objective functions. They invent their own new problems all the time. They change their own objective functions. This whole premise of having systems that don't change their objectives didn't make any sense to me. It was very naive in my point of view. I couldn't sign those letters.

Today we have these extreme cases where people are using AI to fight against each other. If you look at the war between Ukraine and Russia, it's about AI-based drones on this side fighting against AI-based drones on the other side. There's no alignment whatsoever. Of course, you cannot expect in our world a universal government that is going to align all these AIs, because all these different secret services and militaries have different objectives, which are often totally conflicting with each other. It seems to me that all these efforts of the 2010s were kind of naive.

items.question: How do you think about the risks of giving AI systems the freedom to set their own goals?
items.object: The intelligence and safety of AI systems that set their own goals
items.answer:
If you want to get really smart AIs, you have to give them the opportunity to set their own goals, like little artificial scientists that ask a new question about what happens if I do this and how the world responds if I do that. Only if you give them the freedom to ask their own questions and solve their own self-invented problems will they become really smart. On the other hand, they will become less predictable. That is of course the issue being addressed here.

Now people ask, “In a world like that, where you have all kinds of AIs that set themselves their own goals, like they have done in my lab for many decades, isn't that super dangerous?” I think it's not going to be more dangerous than what you have now with humans. Humans also set themselves their own goals all the time and come up with new questions to ask. It is true that my kids are unpredictable. I'm not sure what they are going to do in the future, but at least I can contribute as a parent to making them useful members of society. Whenever they come up with bad experiments, like taking a magnifying glass and focusing the sunlight on a little ant, I'm going to punish them and say, “That's bad. You shouldn't do that.” That's how I taught my kids to become reasonable members of society. The same thing we are going to do with our robots and machines.

In the long run, once they are much smarter than we are, I think we can expect a certain kind of protection through the fact that they are scientists. Artificial scientists will be super interested in life, their own origins and civilization, and everything that led to their current state. They will be fascinated by life and greatly motivated to protect the source of interesting patterns rather than destroy it. From this high-level perspective, I think there's a very strong reason why you shouldn't be too afraid of Arnold Schwarzenegger Terminator scenarios.

items.question: What do you consider the most interesting direction for your AI research today?
items.object: His continuing pursuit of general-purpose AI
items.answer: I'm a conservative guy, and I think the most interesting way of going forward is still the one that I pursued in the '70s and '80s, when I tried to build this general-purpose AI that learns to become smarter than myself such that I can retire. I'm still working on the same old thing.

items.question: What have you learned from your PhD students about what makes a really good researcher?
items.object: The qualities of a good researcher
items.answer: Many of the best PhD students that I have had the pleasure to work with usually focused on a particular question. There's the general big problem that we want to solve, but then there is this particular little thing that currently doesn't work. You have to look at the details: how do these weights change in this neural network, which is trained by this particular learning algorithm, and why doesn't the network do what you want it to do? You have to debug a little tiny thing, and suddenly you see the devil is in the detail. There is a little detail which you have overlooked so far, and if you fix that one, suddenly everything works out and you have a breakthrough. Then the same PhD student can come up with one research paper at a major conference after another, just because it's such a rich source of additional improvements that was triggered by this little devil-in-the-detail solution.

items.question: How do you expect transformer architectures to evolve over the next five to ten years?
items.object: The future of transformer architectures and computational efficiency
items.answer: I guess some sort of transformer will persist, but I think it's going to be a little bit more like the efficient transformer that we had in 1991, the linear transformer. Today it's called the unnormalized linear transformer. I call it the fast weight controller. What's interesting about it? It scales linearly, which means that if you have 1,000 times more text, then you need 1,000 times more compute. The modern quadratic transformer of 2017, if you have 1,000 times more text, you need 1 million times more compute. Everybody's worried about that. It's one of the reasons why these data centers are now so super expensive: you have to do so much compute. Everybody wants to bring down this complexity to a more reasonable linear complexity or maybe log-linear complexity. There are quite a few transformer variants that are going in this direction. You want to get the complexity down, and it's related to what you asked before: intelligence is about doing the same thing with less effort. We want to reduce the effort.

items.question: Why do you consider physical AI operating in the real world so important?
items.object: Physical AI and self-improving robot societies
items.answer:
What I consider the most important stuff is physical AI outside the screen, not behind the screen, but in the real world.

For hundreds of years people have talked about self-replicating machines, but nobody had any idea how to get there. Now we see an opening. For the first time, we now can have—or maybe will soon have—robots that can learn through imitation or reinforcement learning to operate the existing machines, all the existing machines that are already part of our civilization. Once you have a machine that can operate all the machines that humans currently are operating, then you have a new kind of life. You have a way of implementing this ultimate scaling machine, because you can have robots that make more of themselves. I've said that for decades, and now it's getting closer to reality.

You don't need super-smart robots for doing that, just smart enough to learn to operate all the existing machines. A collection of machines like that can make more of itself and can also improve itself, not only make replicas of itself, because all the concepts of machine learning that we already have for AI behind the screen, in the virtual world, we are going to apply to self-improving robot societies. Something like that is not only going to work in the biosphere but also on the moon or on Mercury, where there's a lot of material for building infrastructure and bigger AIs and more AIs and more robots and huge spacecraft and all kinds of stuff that we need to colonize the solar system.

The response characterizes a machine capable of operating all the machines humans currently operate as a new kind of life.
The response argues that robotic self-replication requires only enough intelligence to learn to operate existing machinery, rather than superintelligence.
The response proposes applying machine-learning methods from virtual AI to enable societies of robots to improve themselves.
The response identifies extraterrestrial raw materials as a basis for self-replicating robotic systems to expand beyond Earth.
